title: The Problem-Solution Paradox (Chapter 4)
source: Thomas Wendt, Design for Dasein: Understanding the Design of Experiences (2015), Ch. 4

sections.heading: The Paradox of Design
sections.summary: Design thinking + lean startup share an unresolved tension formalized as the problem-solution paradox; each half (linear vs. praxis) fails alone; the paradox is grounded in non-dualist philosophy (Heidegger's hermeneutic circle, Saussure's chain of signification, Schön's conversation with the situation).

sections.heading: Questioning Design Dualisms
sections.summary: The problem-solution 'dichotomy' is not a dichotomy except under strict dualism; design is not always problem-solving (iPhone/App-Store as unmet-need example); MacCormac/Cross on the brief as exploration; critique of Cartesian 'waterfall'; prototyping/sketching as externalized thought; potentiality/abduction; Martin's reliability vs. validity; Dorst's co-evolution and emergent bridge; paradox-as-antinomy; Morozov's solutionism; Basalla's technological evolution.

sections.heading: Chapter close — antinomies and Latour
sections.summary: Nelson & Stolterman's twelve design paradoxes read as antinomies (contradictions that must be, never optimized to a fixed point); Latour on objects as 'gatherings'/Dinge and design's inability to 'draw together' a thing's full complexity; exploring complexity = the key goal of phenomenological design thinking.

key_terms.gloss: Neither problem nor solution is intelligible without the other; the meta example of a wicked problem.
A problem that defies traditional conceptions of solutions; the paradox is its meta-instance.
Stance that wholes and parts, problem and solution, co-depend; the chapter's governing commitment.
Understanding of the whole depends on the parts and vice versa; phenomenological warrant for co-evolution.
Signs mean only differentially/relationally; linguistic analogue of problem-solution interdependence.
Designing as ongoing exchange with the environment.
Problem space is evolved in the act of producing solutions, not analyzed in advance.
Linear, theory-first, enactment-deferred design; the chapter's foil.
Design grounded in internal/external interaction; rapid prototyping its exemplar.
Disposable object used to think beyond the head, opening an emergent space independent of designer and user.
Designing for possible (not only actual) technical mediations; abduction as the future-facing mode.
Repeatable data vs. valid future-insight; design thinking sits at their intersection.
The two co-evolving notional spaces of creative design.
Joint, iterative development of problem and solution toward a matching pair.
Temporary fix that identifies a problem-solution pairing amid unstable spaces.
A necessary, unsolvable contradiction requiring redefinition rather than resolution.
The disposition to treat the world as a problem to be solved.
Technologies as evolved manifestations of human meaning-making, not isolated solutions.
Twelve paradoxical pole-pairs naming design's irreducible complexity.
Objects as assemblies of controversies and stakeholders that design cannot yet draw together.

claims.text: The problem-solution paradox: we cannot think about solutions until we understand the problem, and we cannot understand a problem until we think about solutions.
The paradox is the meta example of a wicked problem, inherent in all design disciplines and defying traditional conceptions of solutions.
The linear half assumes a 'final answer' at the end of understanding, but design is abductive: designers seek the many context-appropriate truths, not Truth.
Both design thinking's and lean's rebuttals each account for only half of the paradox, so neither escapes it.
The problem-solution dichotomy is not a dichotomy; problems and solutions are wrapped up in one another and each is understood only through the lens of the other.
Introducing solutions into a problem space does not necessarily 'solve' the problem but changes the conditions in which the problem exists.
Design is not always problem-solving; much of the designed world meets a previously unmet (or manufactured) market need, e.g., the 2007 iPhone/App-Store ecosystem.
The design brief is not a specification for a solution but the starting point for an exploration (MacCormac via Cross).
Designers discover or evolve the problem space in the process of creating solutions — the combination of thinking and making.
The waterfall/Cartesian assumption that theory's performance is unnecessary for its validation is at odds with phenomenological design thinking.
A prototype is a disposable pseudo-object used to think beyond the head and to create an emergent space independent of designer and user.
Technological shaping of the lifeworld happens in terms of possible technical mediations, not just actual ones, so designers must design for potentiality.
Creative design generates a matching problem-solution pair through co-evolution, the spaces unstable until temporarily fixed by an emergent bridge (Dorst).
We cannot presuppose that there is something like a set 'design problem' at any point in the design process (Dorst).
The paradox is an antinomy, only a paradox if we assume the movement from problem to solution is linear; its solution is a rethinking of the problem.
Rethinking the nature of a solution means resisting 'solutionism' and reserving effort for genuine wicked problems (Morozov).
Technological objects are not isolated solutions to discrete problems; design should attend to systems and holistic experience (Basalla, qualified as 'a bit extreme').
Design's twelve antinomies are contradictions that must be; collapsing a pole is disastrous and the right balance shifts with context (Nelson & Stolterman).
Objects are assemblies/'gatherings' (Dinge); design cannot yet draw together a thing in all its complexity (Latour).
Exploring the fundamental complexity of design is the key goal of phenomenological design thinking.

interlocutors.name: Kees Dorst
interlocutors.work: Design paradox / co-evolution of problem and solution
interlocutors.draws: Principal positive source: problem space / solution space, co-evolution, emergent bridge, and the 'no set design problem' conclusion.

interlocutors.name: Nigel Cross (quoting Richard MacCormac)
interlocutors.draws: Brief as 'starting point for an exploration' not a specification; sketching as external store supporting the problem-solution dialogue (thinking-and-making, materialized speech object).

interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
interlocutors.work: The Origin of the Work of Art / hermeneutic circle; objects as Dinge
interlocutors.draws: Hermeneutic circle (parts/whole co-dependence) and artwork as non-thingly anchor the non-dualist lineage; 'gatherings'/Dinge frames the closing notion of the thing.

interlocutors.name: Ferdinand de Saussure
interlocutors.draws: Signs have no meaning in themselves; the 'chain of signification' as a non-dualist, relational precedent for problem-solution interdependence.

interlocutors.name: Donald Schön
interlocutors.draws: Design as a conversation with the situation; reflective-practice basis extended via Cross's externalized artifact.

interlocutors.name: Horst Rittel & Melvin Webber
interlocutors.work: Dilemmas in a General Theory of Planning (wicked problems)
interlocutors.draws: First allusion to the paradox; the 'wicked problem' frame and the antinomies of linear problem-to-solution movement.

interlocutors.name: Roger Martin
interlocutors.work: The Design of Business / reliability vs. validity
interlocutors.draws: Reliability vs. validity distinction; design thinking located at their intersection to defend orientation toward potentiality.

interlocutors.name: Evgeny Morozov
interlocutors.draws: 'Solutionism' critique; warrant for rethinking the nature of a solution and reserving effort for wicked problems.

interlocutors.name: George Basalla
interlocutors.draws: Fallacy of technological objects as isolated solutions to discrete problems; evolutionary theory of technology (qualified by Wendt as 'a bit extreme').

interlocutors.name: Harold Nelson & Erik Stolterman
interlocutors.draws: Twelve design paradoxes/antinomies; taxonomy of design's irreducible complexity that must hold both poles.

interlocutors.name: Bruno Latour
interlocutors.work: A Cautious Prometheus? (design and 'drawing things together')
interlocutors.draws: Objects as assemblies/'gatherings'; design's inability to draw together the controversies and stakeholders of a thing — capstone on complexity.

interlocutors.name: Design thinking & lean startup (frameworks)
interlocutors.draws: Not authors but the two frameworks whose shared, unresolved tension launches the chapter and tacitly attempt to address the paradox.

design_principles.name: Resist final answers
design_principles.gloss: Design is abductive; pursue many context-appropriate truths, not Truth.

design_principles.name: Brief as exploration
design_principles.gloss: Treat the brief as a starting point for exploration, not a specification for a solution.

design_principles.name: Thinking and making
design_principles.gloss: Discover/evolve the problem space through creating solutions; do not separate understanding from making.

design_principles.name: Reject the waterfall
design_principles.gloss: Avoid the Cartesian, theory-first, enactment-deferred method; enact early because theory's performance is necessary to its validation.

design_principles.name: Prototype to think beyond the head
design_principles.gloss: Use disposable prototypes/sketches as externalized thought opening an emergent space independent of designer and user.

design_principles.name: Design for potentiality
design_principles.gloss: Orient toward possible technical mediations (speculative design, design fictions); hold present-analysis and future-abduction together.

design_principles.name: Intersect valid and reliable
design_principles.gloss: Do not let quantitative 'illusion of certainty' foreclose the future (Martin).

design_principles.name: Co-evolve toward a matching pair
design_principles.gloss: Generate a problem-solution pair via co-evolution, fixed only temporarily by an emergent bridge; presuppose no fixed design problem.

design_principles.name: Frame anti-dualism as risk management
design_principles.gloss: Recast praxis-based, anti-dualist design as risk mitigation and build the language to articulate co-construction to clients.

design_principles.name: Redefine, don't solve, the antinomy
design_principles.gloss: Treat the paradox as an antinomy to be redefined; rethink the problem rather than force a linear resolution.

design_principles.name: Resist solutionism
design_principles.gloss: Rethink the nature of a solution; reserve effort for genuine wicked problems rather than manufacturing problems for profit.

design_principles.name: Design systems, not isolated solutions
design_principles.gloss: Do not treat technological objects as isolated solutions to discrete problems; design for holistic experience across social/political/economic systems.

design_principles.name: Hold both poles
design_principles.gloss: Maintain both poles of each design antinomy; never optimize to a fixed point, since the right balance shifts with context.

design_principles.name: Draw things together
design_principles.gloss: Aim to represent the controversies, stakeholders, and assemblies of a thing (Latour) — make complexity, not just the object, designable.

ro_hooks.note: Mutual constitution of problem/solution echoes the actualization-of-desire chain's refusal of a fixed first term; object of desire and pursuing act co-specify.
Think-beyond-the-head and the emergent space parallel the ontology's world-involving cognition; the artifact functions as an equipmental mediator of directedness.
Latour's Dinge and Nelson & Stolterman's antinomies model the thing as an irreducible assembly, congenial to modeling a VLE as a relational field of system-effects rather than a discrete target.
